bellman.lead: Bellman's contribution is a way of not enumerating. A sequential decision problem has a number of possible plans that grows exponentially with the horizon; the principle of optimality says that whatever the first action, the remainder must itself be optimal, which turns one exponential search into a recursion over states.

blocks.b:
The principle of optimality states that an optimal policy has the property that, whatever the initial state and first decision, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with respect to the state that results. Because the future depends on the present only through the state, the value of a state can be written in terms of the values of its successors:

$$V^\star(s) = \max_{a} \Big[ R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, V^\star(s') \Big]$$

The discount $\gamma \in [0,1)$ keeps the sum finite over an infinite horizon and expresses a preference for reward sooner. This is a fixed-point equation, and the operator on the right is a contraction in the max norm — so value iteration, repeatedly applying it, converges to the unique $V^\star$ from any starting point, at a rate governed by $\gamma$.

blocks.h: Why it is not a search
blocks.b:
Enumerating policies over a horizon $T$ with $|A|$ actions costs $|A|^T$. The recursion costs one sweep over states per iteration, and the number of iterations depends on the discount rather than on the horizon.

The saving is the same one dynamic programming makes everywhere: overlapping subproblems computed once and reused. What makes it applicable here is the Markov property — the state summarises the past sufficiently that the future does not need it — which is an assumption about the problem, not a property of the method.

Two requirements make the equation inapplicable to most real problems.

It needs the **model**: $P(s' \mid s, a)$ and $R(s,a)$ must be known, because the expectation over successors is computed explicitly. An agent that can act in a world but cannot predict it has nothing to sum over.

And it needs a **table**: one entry per state, swept in full each iteration. Bellman's own phrase for the consequence is the *curse of dimensionality* — a state described by $d$ variables with $k$ values each has $k^d$ entries, so a modest description makes the table larger than any memory.

Everything else in this lane is a response to one or both. Temporal-difference learning removes the model by sampling transitions instead of summing over them. Function approximation, eventually a neural network, removes the table by generalising across states rather than storing them.

The equation itself is still what modern methods are estimating. A Q-learning update is a sampled, incremental application of it; a critic in an actor-critic method is a learned approximation of $V$; the target in DQN's regression is the right-hand side with the expectation replaced by one sampled successor.

So this node is not a historical preliminary but the object every value-based method in the lane is approximating. The differences between them are entirely in how they cope with not having the model and not being able to afford the table.

td.lead: Dynamic programming needs a model to take the expectation over successors, and Monte Carlo estimation needs an episode to finish before it can learn anything. Temporal-difference learning takes one step from each: sample the transition as Monte Carlo does, and bootstrap from the current estimate as dynamic programming does.

blocks.h: Learning a guess from a guess
blocks.b:
After observing a transition $s \to s'$ with reward $r$, update towards the one-step estimate:

$$V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha \big[\underbrace{r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)}_{\text{TD error } \delta}\big]$$

The target $r + \gamma V(s')$ uses a sampled successor, so no model is needed, and it uses the current estimate of $V(s')$, so no episode has to finish. Sutton's phrase for it is learning a guess from a guess.

Both halves matter. Monte Carlo waits for the actual return, which is unbiased and high-variance and unavailable until termination — useless for a continuing task. Dynamic programming uses the exact expectation, which is low-variance and requires the transition model. TD is biased, because $V(s')$ is wrong early on, and its variance is far lower than Monte Carlo's because it involves one random transition rather than a whole trajectory.

One-step TD propagates information slowly: a reward at the end of a long corridor moves back one state per episode. Monte Carlo propagates it all at once and pays in variance.

TD($\lambda$) interpolates. Each state keeps an **eligibility trace** that decays by $\gamma\lambda$ per step and is bumped when the state is visited, and the TD error updates every state in proportion to its trace:

$$e_t(s) = \gamma \lambda \, e_{t-1}(s) + \mathbb{1}[s_t = s], \qquad V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha \, \delta_t \, e_t(s)$$

At $\lambda = 0$ this is one-step TD; at $\lambda = 1$ it is equivalent to Monte Carlo. The parameter is a dial between bias and variance, and the trace is what makes the intermediate settings implementable online with $O(|S|)$ memory rather than by storing trajectories.

For a fixed policy with tabular values and a suitably decaying step size, TD(0) converges to the true $V^\pi$. That is a real guarantee and its conditions are restrictive: tabular representation, and a policy that is not changing.

With function approximation the guarantee weakens sharply. Off-policy learning, bootstrapping and function approximation together — Sutton and Barto's **deadly triad** — can diverge, and simple counterexamples exist where the value estimate grows without bound. Every method in this lane that uses all three, DQN included, is operating outside what is proved, which is why its stabilisers are engineering rather than theory.

The signal $\delta$ turned out to be more general than the algorithm. It is the quantity prioritised replay ranks transitions by, the advantage estimate an actor-critic method uses as its baseline-corrected return, and the term generalised advantage estimation smooths over multiple horizons.

It also has a well-documented correspondence with the firing of dopamine neurons in response to unexpected reward, which is one of the closer contacts between this field and neuroscience — and which is why the algorithm is sometimes described as a model of prediction rather than merely a method for it.

qlearn.lead: TD learning evaluates the policy that generated the data. Q-learning evaluates the best policy regardless of what generated the data, by taking a max over actions in its target — which makes it **off-policy**, and means an agent can learn the optimal behaviour while behaving otherwise.

blocks.b:
Q-learning estimates action values rather than state values, and its update is

$$Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\Big[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\Big]$$

The target refers to $\max_{a'} Q(s', a')$, not to the action the agent actually took next. So the values converge towards $Q^\star$ — the optimal action-value function — no matter which policy is being followed, provided every state-action pair keeps being visited.

Watkins and Dayan's convergence proof makes this precise for the tabular case with a decaying step size and infinite visitation. It is one of the few strong guarantees in the field, and it explains why Q-learning became the default: the agent may explore as badly as it likes and still learn the right values.

blocks.h: Why action values rather than state values
blocks.b:
Learning $V$ is not enough to act. Choosing an action from a state value requires knowing where each action leads — the model again — whereas $\arg\max_a Q(s,a)$ is a lookup.

That is the trade: $Q$ has $|S| \times |A|$ entries against $V$'s $|S|$, and in exchange the policy is available without a model. For control rather than prediction, this is what makes model-free learning possible at all, and it is why the value-based line of this lane is built on $Q$.

The same operator that makes the method off-policy also makes it optimistic. $\mathbb{E}[\max_a Q] \geq \max_a \mathbb{E}[Q]$, so taking a maximum over noisy estimates systematically overestimates — the noise in whichever action happens to be overrated is what gets selected and propagated.

With a tabular representation and decaying noise this washes out. With function approximation, where errors are correlated across states and do not vanish, it compounds: overestimates propagate through the bootstrap into further overestimates. This is the specific defect Double DQN addresses, and the reason twin critics appear in TD3 and SAC.

Exploration is also left entirely outside the algorithm. Convergence assumes every pair is visited infinitely often; nothing in the update makes that happen, so $\epsilon$-greedy or something better must be bolted on.

The table is the binding constraint. Backgammon has $10^{20}$ states, Atari from pixels has more than there are atoms in the observable universe, and no amount of memory helps because the agent must also visit each one.

The answer is function approximation — replace the table with a parameterised $Q_\theta(s,a)$ that generalises across similar states — and for two decades that combination was known to be unstable, since off-policy learning, bootstrapping and function approximation together form the deadly triad. DQN is where the combination was made to work, not by resolving the instability but by engineering around it with a replay buffer and a frozen target network.

dqn.lead: Q-learning with a neural function approximator was known to diverge, and had for two decades. DQN makes it work on Atari from raw pixels with two mechanisms that attack the instability rather than the algorithm — a replay buffer that decorrelates the updates, and a frozen copy of the network that holds the regression target still.

blocks.b:
Two problems compound. Consecutive frames in an episode are nearly identical, so online updates are made on highly correlated samples — a violation of the independence stochastic gradient descent assumes, and one that lets the network overwrite what it learned moments earlier as the data distribution shifts with the policy.

And the regression target $r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta)$ is computed from the network being updated. Every gradient step moves the target, so the network chases its own output — a feedback loop with no fixed point that the optimiser can settle into.

Either alone is manageable. Together, with a function approximator whose errors are correlated across states, they diverge.

**Experience replay** stores transitions $(s, a, r, s')$ in a large buffer and samples minibatches uniformly at random. Consecutive samples in a batch come from different episodes and different times, so the correlation is broken, and each transition is reused many times rather than seen once — a large gain in sample efficiency, and the reason the method must be off-policy, since the buffer contains data from old policies.

**A target network** $Q^-$ is a copy of the weights, frozen and refreshed every few thousand steps. The regression target becomes

$$y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^-(s', a')$$

so between refreshes the problem is ordinary supervised regression against a fixed target. The delay is what converts a moving fixed point into a sequence of stationary ones.

The input is four stacked greyscale frames, downsampled — stacking because a single frame does not reveal velocity, so the state would not be Markov without it. The architecture is a small convolutional stack in AlexNet's idiom with a fully connected head, and the output is one $Q$-value per action rather than a class distribution, so a single forward pass scores every action.

Rewards are clipped to $[-1, 1]$ so that one learning rate serves games with wildly different score scales. This is a practical necessity and a real distortion — it flattens genuine differences in reward magnitude, so the agent cannot tell a small win from a large one.

The same architecture and hyperparameters are used for every game, with only the action count differing, which is the result that made the paper: one learner, no per-task feature engineering, human-level or better play on a majority of the suite.

blocks.h: What it left for its successors
blocks.b:
Each of DQN's known defects became a paper. The $\max$ operator's overestimation bias, present since Q-learning and made worse by approximation — Double DQN. Uniform sampling from the buffer, which spends most of its updates on transitions the agent has already mastered — prioritised replay. One output head conflating how good a state is with how much the action matters — duelling architectures. $\epsilon$-greedy exploration, which is action noise rather than directed curiosity — noisy networks. Rainbow then shows the six of them are complementary.

The deeper limitation is that DQN is enormously sample-hungry — tens of millions of frames for games a person learns in minutes — and confined to discrete action sets, since $\arg\max$ over a continuous action space is itself an optimisation. That second constraint is what the deterministic policy gradient line exists to remove.

ddqn.lead: Q-learning's target takes a maximum over noisy estimates, and the maximum of noisy estimates is biased upward. Double DQN fixes it with a change of one line: use the online network to choose the action and the target network to score it, so the noise that selects is not the noise that evaluates.

blocks.b:
For any set of noisy estimates, $\mathbb{E}[\max_a Q(s,a)] \geq \max_a \mathbb{E}[Q(s,a)]$, with equality only if the estimates are exact. The $\max$ selects whichever action happens to be overrated by noise, so the target inherits that error rather than averaging it away.

The bootstrap then compounds it. An inflated target raises $Q(s,a)$, which becomes the target for its predecessors, which raises them in turn. Van Hasselt et al. measure this on Atari and find value estimates diverging far above any achievable return — the agent believing it will score orders of magnitude more than the game permits.

Crucially the bias is not uniform across actions, so it does not cancel in the policy: it distorts which action looks best, not merely how good everything looks.

The standard DQN target is $y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^-(s', a')$, where one network both picks and scores.

Double DQN uses two:

$$y = r + \gamma \, Q^-\Big(s', \; \arg\max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta)\Big)$$

The online network $\theta$ names the action; the frozen target network $\theta^-$ says what it is worth. If the online network overrates an action through noise, the target network — trained on different data at a different time — will not usually share that error, so the inflated estimate is not confirmed.

DQN already maintains a target network, so this costs nothing: the same two networks, evaluated in a different arrangement. That is the appeal — a bias correction with no new machinery and no new hyperparameter.

blocks.h: What it does and does not remove
blocks.b:
Value estimates become far more accurate against the true returns, and scores improve across much of the Atari suite. The paper's more interesting demonstration is that better values and better policies go together here, which is not automatic — a uniformly wrong value function can still induce the right ranking.

The correction is partial. The two networks are not independent: $\theta^-$ is a delayed copy of $\theta$, so their errors are correlated, and the longer the delay the weaker the correlation but the staler the target. Overestimation is reduced, not eliminated, and van Hasselt is explicit about this.

The fully decoupled version — two networks trained on disjoint data — is what TD3's twin critics approximate in continuous control, using the minimum of two independently initialised critics rather than a delayed copy. That it was still worth doing three years later says the problem was not settled here.

Double DQN is the first of the six components Rainbow assembles, and the one with the clearest diagnosis behind it — a named statistical bias, measured, with a targeted correction.

It is also a good illustration of how this part of the lane proceeds. DQN made the combination work; each subsequent paper isolates one defect of it, fixes that defect and leaves the rest alone; and Rainbow's contribution is showing that the fixes compose rather than overlap.

dueling.lead: A single output head has to learn, for every state and action, how much total return follows. Most of that number is a property of the state and has nothing to do with the action. The duelling architecture splits the estimate into those two parts, so the state's value is learned once rather than separately under each action.

blocks.b:
Define the advantage $A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s)$: how much better this action is than the state's average. In many states the answer is "barely at all" — an Atari frame with nothing nearby has the same outcome whatever the joystick does.

A standard network must nonetheless learn $Q(s,a)$ separately for each $a$, and each of those estimates carries the whole of $V(s)$. The information is duplicated $|A|$ times and each copy is learned only from the transitions where that action was taken.

The duelling network computes both streams from shared convolutional features — a scalar $V(s)$ and a vector $A(s,a)$ — and combines them into $Q$. Now $V(s)$ is updated by **every** transition from that state, whichever action was taken, which is where the sample-efficiency gain comes from.

The naive combination $Q(s,a) = V(s) + A(s,a)$ is not identifiable: adding a constant to $V$ and subtracting it from every $A$ leaves $Q$ unchanged, so the two streams can drift arbitrarily and nothing pins them down.

The fix is to force the advantage to have zero mean over actions:

$$Q(s, a) = V(s) + \Big(A(s, a) - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{a'} A(s, a')\Big)$$

Subtracting the maximum instead is the theoretically cleaner choice — it makes $V$ exactly the value of the greedy action — but the paper reports the mean version more stable, because its target moves less when the greedy action changes. It is a case where the less principled option was kept for a stated empirical reason.

The gain concentrates in states with many actions of similar value, which is most states in most games, and the paper's saliency visualisations show the two streams attending to different things: the value stream to the horizon and the score, the advantage stream to immediate obstacles.

Where actions genuinely differ, there is little to share and the architecture reduces to a more elaborate way of computing the same thing. The benefit therefore scales with the action count and with how often the choice is inconsequential.

It is a pure architectural change — the loss, the replay buffer and the target network are all DQN's — which is why it composes with Double DQN and prioritised replay without interaction, and why Rainbow can adopt all three at once.

Separating state value from action advantage outlived the architecture. Advantage is the quantity actor-critic methods estimate rather than raw returns, precisely because subtracting the state's value removes variance that carries no information about the action; generalised advantage estimation is a smoothed version of the same idea across horizons.

So this node's contribution is less the two-headed network than the observation that $Q$ is mostly $V$, and that the part which is not is the only part a policy needs.

per.lead: DQN's replay buffer samples uniformly, so a transition the agent has already mastered is drawn as often as one it still gets wrong. Prioritised replay ranks transitions by the size of their TD error and samples the surprising ones more — and then has to correct the bias that introduces.

blocks.b:
The magnitude of the TD error, $|\delta| = |r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^-(s',a') - Q(s,a)|$, measures how wrong the current estimate was about that transition. A large error means there is something still to learn from it; a small one means the network already agrees with its own target.

Sampling proportionally to $|\delta|$ alone is too aggressive — a transition whose error is momentarily zero would never be revisited, and outliers would dominate — so the priority is softened and floored:

$$P(i) = \frac{p_i^{\alpha}}{\sum_k p_k^{\alpha}}, \qquad p_i = |\delta_i| + \epsilon$$

with $\alpha$ interpolating between uniform sampling at $0$ and fully greedy at $1$. A rank-based variant, using $1/\mathrm{rank}$, is more robust to outliers at similar cost.

Q-learning's update assumes samples are drawn from the distribution the loss is defined over. Sampling by priority changes that distribution, so the gradient estimate is biased — the network is fitted to a reweighted version of the data.

Importance sampling corrects it:

$$w_i = \left(\frac{1}{N} \cdot \frac{1}{P(i)}\right)^{\beta}$$

applied as a weight on each transition's update and normalised by $\max_i w_i$ for stability. The exponent $\beta$ is annealed from a value below one towards one over training, so the bias is tolerated early — when the estimates are wrong anyway and speed matters more — and removed by the end, when the solution is being fixed.

Maintaining the distribution efficiently needs a data structure: a sum-tree gives $O(\log N)$ sampling and priority updates over a buffer of a million transitions.

Priorities are stale by construction. A transition's $|\delta|$ is recorded when it is sampled, and every subsequent gradient step changes what its error would be now — so the buffer is ranked by a snapshot that ages. New transitions are inserted at maximum priority to guarantee they are seen at least once, which is a heuristic rather than a fix.

Two more hyperparameters appear, $\alpha$ and the $\beta$ schedule, and they interact with the learning rate: prioritisation effectively raises the magnitude of updates on high-error transitions, so the paper reduces the step size when using it.

The gains are nonetheless substantial and broad across Atari, and the mechanism is the reason curriculum-like effects appear without any curriculum being specified — the buffer naturally focuses on the frontier of what the agent has not yet learned.

Sampling proportional to error is not specific to reinforcement learning. Hard example mining in detection is the same instinct, and the focal loss is a continuous version of it — reweight rather than resample, so nothing is discarded and no importance correction is needed.

Within this lane, prioritised replay is one of Rainbow's six components and among the ones whose removal costs most in the ablation, alongside multi-step returns.

noisy.lead: $\epsilon$-greedy explores by ignoring what the network thinks and acting at random, which is undirected and gets no better as the agent learns. Noisy networks add learnable noise to the weights instead, so exploration is a property of the policy that the gradient can shape and shrink where it is no longer useful.

blocks.h: Noise in the parameters, not the action
blocks.b:
A noisy linear layer replaces each weight with a mean plus a scaled random perturbation:

$$y = (\mu^w + \sigma^w \odot \varepsilon^w)\, x + (\mu^b + \sigma^b \odot \varepsilon^b)$$

where $\varepsilon$ is resampled per forward pass and $\mu, \sigma$ are trained by ordinary backpropagation. The gradient reaches $\sigma$ through the reparameterisation, exactly as in a VAE, so the network learns how much noise each weight should carry.

The difference from action noise is consistency across a trajectory. Perturbing the parameters once per episode gives a coherent alternative policy — the agent commits to behaving differently for a while — whereas $\epsilon$-greedy makes an independent random choice at each step, which for a task needing a sustained deviation is close to useless.

Independent noise per weight means $p \times q$ random numbers per layer per forward pass, which is expensive to generate. **Factorised Gaussian noise** draws $p + q$ samples instead and forms the matrix as an outer product of transformed vectors, $\varepsilon^w_{ij} = f(\varepsilon_i)f(\varepsilon_j)$ with $f(x) = \mathrm{sgn}(x)\sqrt{|x|}$.

The cost falls from quadratic to linear in layer width at a small loss of expressiveness. This is the version used for the large single-threaded agents; the fully independent form is kept for the distributed ones where noise generation is not the bottleneck.

The interesting property is what happens to $\sigma$ over training. Where extra exploration no longer pays, the gradient drives it towards zero and the layer becomes deterministic; where the agent still benefits from variability it stays large. The paper shows this happening at different rates in different games, with no schedule specified anywhere.

That replaces the $\epsilon$ decay schedule — a hyperparameter that had to be tuned per task and could not adapt within a task — with something learned. It is a small change with an outsized effect on games requiring sustained exploration, which is where $\epsilon$-greedy fails most visibly.

The costs are that every noisy layer doubles its parameters, and that the noise is in weight space rather than in a space that means anything — there is no guarantee that a perturbation corresponds to a sensible alternative strategy, only that it is consistent.

Noisy networks are the exploration component of Rainbow, replacing $\epsilon$-greedy entirely. The ablation there finds it useful but not among the largest contributors, and its benefit is concentrated in the hard-exploration games rather than spread evenly.

The broader point it makes is that exploration should be part of the learned policy rather than a wrapper around it, which is also the argument maximum-entropy methods make from the other direction — SAC puts an entropy term in the objective so the policy is rewarded for staying stochastic, rather than having stochasticity injected.

rainbow.lead: Six independent improvements to DQN had each been published against the same baseline, and nobody knew whether they overlapped. Rainbow puts all six in one agent, shows they largely compose, and — through a systematic ablation — reports which ones the result actually depends on.

blocks.b:
**Double Q-learning** decouples action selection from evaluation to reduce the max operator's optimistic bias. **Prioritised replay** samples transitions by TD error rather than uniformly. **Duelling networks** split the head into state value and action advantage. **Multi-step returns** bootstrap after $n$ steps rather than one, trading a little bias for much faster reward propagation. **Distributional RL** — C51 — predicts a distribution over returns on a fixed support of atoms instead of a scalar expectation. **Noisy networks** replace $\epsilon$-greedy with learned parametric noise.

Each addresses a different defect, which is the paper's implicit hypothesis: the six are orthogonal, so applying them together should be roughly additive rather than redundant.

The combination is not purely mechanical, because several of the components define what the loss is. Distributional RL replaces the squared TD error with a KL divergence between projected distributions, so prioritised replay — which ranks by $|\delta|$ — has to rank by that KL term instead.

Multi-step returns fold into the distributional target by shifting and scaling the support. The duelling architecture is applied to the distributional output, splitting into value and advantage **streams over atoms**. And noisy layers replace the linear layers of both streams.

So the paper is partly an integration exercise, and the fact that the pieces can be made mutually consistent is a result in itself.

The combined agent substantially exceeds every individual variant on the Atari suite, in both final score and data efficiency, and the ablation — removing one component at a time — is the more useful contribution.

Prioritised replay and multi-step returns are the two whose removal costs most, consistently across games. The distributional loss matters, with its contribution growing later in training. Noisy networks help, unevenly, concentrated in hard-exploration games. Duelling and double Q-learning are the smallest, and duelling's removal is close to neutral in the combined agent even though it clearly helps a plain DQN.

That last finding is the interesting one: a component's value depends on what else is present. Duelling reduces variance in value estimation, and the distributional head is already doing something similar, so the two overlap in a way the individual papers could not have revealed.

blocks.h: What it settled and what it did not
blocks.b:
Rainbow became the reference value-based agent and the default baseline for the years following, and it established the practice of ablating a combination rather than reporting only the total.

What it does not address is the sample efficiency of the whole family. Rainbow still needs tens of millions of frames for games a person learns in minutes, and none of the six components changes that by an order of magnitude — they improve the constant. The later data-efficient variants alter the training regime rather than the algorithm, and the model-based line attacks the problem differently by learning a simulator to practise in.

reinforce.lead: Value-based methods learn what states are worth and derive a policy by maximising over actions, which requires the action set to be enumerable and makes the policy a discontinuous function of the values. REINFORCE optimises the policy directly, by an estimator that needs only the ability to sample from it and score the outcome.

blocks.b:
The objective is expected return, $J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}[R(\tau)]$, and the difficulty is that the distribution being averaged over depends on the parameters. The identity $\nabla_\theta p_\theta = p_\theta \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta$ converts that into an expectation that can be sampled:

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}\Big[R(\tau) \sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\Big]$$

The reward need not be differentiable, and the environment need not be known — $R$ enters only as a scalar multiplying the log-probability gradient. In words: increase the probability of the actions taken in trajectories that turned out well, decrease it for the others.

This is the same estimator that appears throughout machine learning wherever an expectation's parameters must be differentiated and reparameterisation is unavailable.

The estimator is unbiased and its variance is severe, because $R(\tau)$ is a sum over a whole trajectory and its scale has nothing to do with the individual action being credited. If every return is large and positive, every action's probability is increased, and learning depends on small differences between large numbers.

Subtracting any function of the state leaves the estimator unbiased, since $\mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)] = 0$:

$$\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}\Big[\big(R(\tau) - b(s_t)\big) \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\Big]$$

The variance-minimising choice is close to the state's expected return, so $b(s) \approx V(s)$, and now the multiplier is *how much better than usual* rather than *how good*. Williams' paper introduces the baseline alongside the estimator; learning it with a second network is what makes the method an actor-critic.

Three things value-based methods cannot easily provide. **Continuous actions** are natural, since the policy is a distribution over $\mathbb{R}^d$ rather than a table to maximise over. **Stochastic policies** are representable, which matters in partially observed and adversarial settings where the optimal behaviour is genuinely mixed. And the policy changes **smoothly** with its parameters, whereas an $\arg\max$ over values can flip discontinuously on a small value change.

The convergence properties differ correspondingly: policy gradient ascends a smooth objective to a local optimum, which is weaker than Q-learning's guarantee of the global optimum in the tabular case and far more robust once function approximation is involved.

blocks.h: The costs that shaped what followed
blocks.b:
REINFORCE is **on-policy** — the expectation is over trajectories from the current policy, so every gradient step invalidates the data that produced it. There is no replay buffer, and sample efficiency is poor.

Variance remains high even with a baseline, since the return is still a Monte Carlo estimate over a full trajectory. Actor-critic methods replace it with a bootstrapped estimate, trading variance for bias.

And the step size is treacherous. A policy update changes the distribution of states the agent visits, so a step that is too large can move to a region where the new policy performs badly and the data to recover is no longer being collected. That failure — not variance — is what TRPO and PPO are built to prevent.

ac.lead: REINFORCE multiplies each action's log-probability gradient by the return of the whole trajectory, which is unbiased and extremely noisy. Actor-critic keeps the policy gradient and replaces that return with a learned value estimate — a critic — trading a small bias for a large reduction in variance.

blocks.b:
The **actor** is the policy $\pi_\theta$, updated by the policy gradient. The **critic** is a value function $V_w$ or $Q_w$, updated by temporal-difference learning. Neither is sufficient alone: the critic cannot act without a max over actions, and the actor without the critic is REINFORCE.

The policy gradient theorem provides the form the actor's update takes with any such estimate substituted for the return:

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\Big[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\; Q^{\pi}(s, a)\Big]$$

and the practical version uses the **advantage** $A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s)$, estimated in one step as the TD error $\delta = r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)$. So the actor is told, for each action, how much better than average it turned out — the baseline of REINFORCE, now learned rather than fixed.

blocks.h: Why the bias is worth it
blocks.b:
A Monte Carlo return is a sum of many random rewards and transitions, so its variance grows with the horizon. A one-step TD estimate involves one transition and one bootstrapped value, so its variance is bounded by the reward scale — but it inherits whatever error is in $V_w$.

The trade is favourable because the critic's error is systematic and shrinking, while Monte Carlo's variance is irreducible. The intermediate settings are available too: an $n$-step return bootstraps after $n$ steps, and generalised advantage estimation averages over all $n$ with a geometric weight $\lambda$, giving the same bias-variance dial that TD($\lambda$) provides for prediction.

The cost is that a wrong critic biases the actor's gradient in a way no amount of data corrects while the critic remains wrong — the two are coupled, and instability in one propagates.

The theory has a condition worth naming. Substituting an arbitrary learned $Q_w$ for $Q^\pi$ makes the gradient biased in general. It is unbiased if the critic is **compatible** — its features are the policy's score function, $\nabla_w Q_w(s,a) = \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)$ — and it is fitted by least squares against the true values.

In practice this condition is ignored: critics are ordinary neural networks with their own architecture. The result is a method whose theoretical guarantee does not apply to any implementation of it, which is a recurring situation in this lane and worth stating rather than glossing.

Actor-critic is the structure of nearly every policy-based method that followed. A3C parallelises the data collection; TRPO and PPO constrain how far the actor may move per update; DDPG and TD3 make the actor deterministic so the critic's gradient with respect to the action can be used directly; SAC adds an entropy term to the objective.

All of them are an actor and a critic with a different answer to the same two questions — how to estimate the advantage, and how far to trust it.

a2c.lead: DQN's replay buffer decorrelates its updates and forces the method to be off-policy, which rules out policy gradients. A3C gets the decorrelation a different way: run many copies of the environment at once, so a batch contains samples from different states of different episodes, and no buffer is needed.

blocks.h: Parallel environments instead of a buffer
blocks.b:
The problem replay solves is that consecutive transitions in one episode are highly correlated. A buffer breaks that by mixing across time, which requires storing old data and therefore learning off-policy.

Running $N$ environment copies breaks it across **space** instead. At any moment the workers are in unrelated states, so a batch assembled from one step of each is already decorrelated, and every sample is fresh — generated by the current policy. On-policy methods become usable at scale, and with them the whole policy-gradient family.

The practical consequence the paper emphasises is hardware: A3C trained on a multi-core CPU in less wall-clock time than GPU-based DQN needed, which changed who could run these experiments.

In **A3C** each worker holds its own copy of the parameters, computes gradients on its own rollout, and applies them to a shared parameter server without waiting — Hogwild-style, with no lock. Workers are therefore slightly out of date with each other, and the paper argues this staleness acts as an additional decorrelating and regularising effect.

The synchronous variant, **A2C**, was found to work as well or better. All workers step together, their gradients are averaged, and one update is applied. It removes the stale-gradient complication, and — decisively for later practice — the batched forward passes use a GPU efficiently, where asynchronous workers cannot.

That A2C matches A3C suggests the asynchrony was never doing the work; the parallelism was.

Three details recur in everything downstream. Returns are **$n$-step** rather than one-step, bootstrapping after a fixed rollout length, which propagates reward faster than TD(0) at a modest cost in bias.

An **entropy bonus** is added to the objective, rewarding the policy for staying uncertain and discouraging premature collapse onto one action — exploration expressed in the loss rather than injected as noise, which is the direction SAC later takes much further.

And actor and critic **share** most of their network, with two heads. That halves the compute and couples the two losses, so their relative weighting becomes a hyperparameter that matters.

On-policy means every sample is used for one gradient step and discarded, because after the update the data no longer comes from the current policy. A3C is therefore far less sample-efficient than DQN per environment interaction, and its advantage is in wall-clock time when environment steps are cheap.

That trade defines where the family is used: simulation, where interactions are nearly free, rather than robotics, where they are not. It is also why the off-policy continuous-control line — DDPG, TD3, SAC — exists in parallel, and why PPO's central contribution is squeezing several gradient steps out of each batch before the on-policy assumption breaks down.

OpenAI Baselines: ACKTR & A2C

trpo.lead: A supervised learner that takes too large a step gets a worse loss and recovers next batch. A policy that takes too large a step changes the states it visits, so the data needed to recover is no longer being collected. TRPO bounds how far the policy may move per update, in the distribution's own geometry rather than in parameter space.

blocks.h: Why a step size is not enough
blocks.b:
The same change in parameters can mean anything about the resulting behaviour: a small step can flip a near-deterministic policy's preferred action, and a large one can barely move a diffuse policy. Euclidean distance in $\theta$ says nothing about distance between the distributions $\pi_\theta$ induces.

The failure that follows is not merely slow learning. Performance collapses, and because the agent's own policy generates its training data, the collapse is self-sustaining — a bad policy visits uninformative states and produces data that cannot repair it. This is the specific instability policy-gradient methods suffer that supervised learning does not.

TRPO's theoretical starting point is a bound: the true return of a new policy is at least a surrogate objective computed under the old one, minus a penalty in their KL divergence. Optimising that bound guarantees monotonic improvement. The penalty coefficient the theory prescribes is far too conservative to be useful, so the practical algorithm converts it into a hard constraint:

$$\max_{\theta} \; \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\pi_\theta(a \mid s)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)} \, \hat{A}\right] \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbb{E}\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\text{old}} \,\|\, \pi_\theta)\big] \leq \delta$$

The ratio is importance sampling, which lets one batch of data score a policy that did not generate it. The constraint is in distribution space, so $\delta$ means the same thing at every point in training and across architectures — which is why TRPO is unusually insensitive to hyperparameters.

The constrained problem is solved by a second-order method. The KL constraint is approximated quadratically, whose matrix is the Fisher information; the objective linearly. The resulting natural-gradient direction is obtained by **conjugate gradient**, which needs only Fisher-vector products — computable by a double backward pass, never forming the matrix — and a **line search** along it enforces the constraint exactly, since the quadratic approximation is only local.

The line search is what makes the guarantee hold in practice rather than approximately: a step is accepted only if it improves the surrogate and satisfies the KL bound.

TRPO gave the first reliable policy-gradient results on continuous control and on Atari from pixels, and its trust-region framing is the ancestor of everything in the family since.

The machinery is the objection. Conjugate gradient, Fisher-vector products and a line search per update are a substantial implementation burden, they interact badly with parameter sharing between actor and critic, and they do not extend cleanly to architectures with recurrence or complex structure.

PPO's contribution is to get most of the benefit from a first-order objective — clip the importance ratio so the surrogate itself stops rewarding large moves — which is why PPO and not TRPO became the default.

refs.t: Trust Region Policy Optimization
A Natural Policy Gradient

ppo.lead: TRPO's trust region works and requires conjugate gradient, Fisher-vector products and a line search on every update. PPO gets a comparable effect from a first-order objective: clip the importance ratio so that moving too far stops improving the surrogate, and the constraint enforces itself through the gradient.

blocks.b:
Let $r_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) / \pi_{\text{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)$. The objective is

$$L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\Big[\min\big(r_t(\theta)\hat{A}_t, \; \mathrm{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_t\big)\Big]$$

with $\epsilon = 0.2$ typically. The $\min$ is what makes it work, and it is asymmetric on purpose. When the advantage is positive, increasing $r_t$ beyond $1+\epsilon$ gives no further gain, so there is no incentive to push the action's probability arbitrarily high from one batch. When the advantage is negative, decreasing $r_t$ below $1-\epsilon$ likewise stops helping.

But the $\min$ leaves the objective **unclipped in the direction that undoes a bad step**: if the ratio has already moved far the wrong way, the gradient still pulls it back. The clip removes the reward for going too far without removing the ability to return.

The practical gain is sample reuse. An on-policy method normally takes one gradient step per batch, because after the update the data no longer comes from the current policy. The importance ratio corrects for that mismatch, and the clip bounds how badly the correction can behave, so PPO runs several epochs of minibatch updates over the same rollout before collecting more.

That is worth several times the data efficiency of a plain policy gradient, and it is why PPO sits where it does — not as efficient as an off-policy method with a replay buffer, but far better than A2C, with none of the instability that off-policy value learning brings.

The full objective adds a value-function loss and an entropy bonus, and advantages are estimated with GAE, which supplies the bias-variance dial through $\lambda$.

blocks.h: How much of it is the clip
blocks.b:
PPO became the default policy-gradient algorithm, used from continuous control to Dota to the RLHF pipelines that fine-tune language models, largely because it is simple to implement and forgiving.

Later analysis complicated the story. Careful ablations found that a substantial share of PPO's advantage over TRPO comes from implementation details reported as incidental — observation and reward normalisation, orthogonal initialisation, learning-rate annealing, gradient clipping, the specific advantage normalisation — rather than from the clipped objective itself. Reproducing published numbers turns out to depend on those details, and the clip alone does not guarantee the trust region: nothing bounds the KL divergence, and it can grow past any intended limit within an epoch.

That is worth stating plainly. The algorithm is excellent and the mechanism credited for it is doing less of the work than the paper implies.

PPO's second life is in language-model alignment, where it optimises a policy against a learned reward model with a KL penalty to a reference policy — InstructGPT's pipeline and every RLHF system derived from it.

In that setting its costs became conspicuous: a value network the size of the policy, four models in memory at once, and considerable sensitivity to the reward model's flaws. GRPO removes the value network by estimating the baseline from a group of sampled responses to the same prompt, and DPO removes the reinforcement learning stage altogether — both responses to PPO's weight rather than to its behaviour.

Implementation Matters in Deep RL: A Case Study on PPO and TRPO
High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation

grpo.lead: PPO needs a critic to supply the baseline, and in language-model fine-tuning that critic is a second network the size of the policy. GRPO removes it: sample a group of responses to the same prompt, score them all, and use the group's own mean as the baseline.

blocks.b:
A policy gradient needs a baseline to subtract, or the variance is unusable. PPO learns one — a value network trained to predict the return from each state, which for a language model means a full-size transformer trained alongside the policy.

GRPO observes that for a prompt with a verifiable or scorable answer, one can simply sample $G$ responses and compare them to each other. The advantage of response $i$ is its reward standardised within its own group:

$$\hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r_1, \ldots, r_G)}{\mathrm{std}(r_1, \ldots, r_G)}\,$$

The mean is an unbiased estimate of the expected reward for that prompt — exactly what the value network was approximating — computed from samples rather than learned. Dividing by the standard deviation normalises across prompts of differing difficulty, so an easy prompt where every response scores well contributes little signal, which is the right behaviour.

In a PPO-based RLHF setup four models are resident: the policy, the reference policy for the KL penalty, the reward model, and the value network. Dropping the value network removes roughly a quarter of the memory and all of the compute spent training it, along with a source of error — a badly fitted critic biases every update, and critics for language models are hard to fit because the return is a single scalar at the end of a long sequence.

The cost is $G$ samples per prompt instead of one. For domains where the reward is a cheap programmatic check — a maths answer against a reference, a unit test against generated code — that trade is strongly favourable, because generation is the affordable part and reward evaluation is nearly free.

The KL penalty to the reference policy is kept, and GRPO applies it as a separate term in the objective rather than folding it into the reward, which the paper argues is better behaved.

The design assumes several responses to one prompt can be meaningfully compared, which is natural when correctness is checkable and less so when the reward is a learned model of human preference over open-ended text — there the group's mean is an estimate from a noisy scorer, and the variance normalisation can amplify noise on prompts where all responses are similar.

GRPO's prominence comes from reasoning models trained with verifiable rewards, where it has been the workhorse. That is the regime it was designed in, and the further it moves from checkable answers the more its advantage over a well-fitted critic narrows.

It also inherits the on-policy sampling cost: $G$ generations per prompt per update, with long outputs, which is not cheap even if it is cheaper than training a critic.

GRPO is one of three answers to the same complaint about PPO in alignment. DPO removes the reinforcement-learning loop entirely, deriving a supervised objective on preference pairs from the same KL-regularised optimum. Rejection sampling and best-of-$n$ fine-tuning simplify differently, by generating, filtering and training supervised.

GRPO keeps the RL loop and deletes the critic, which places it between the two — more machinery than DPO, more exploration than a supervised filter, and the option to keep improving on-policy that neither offers.

dpg.lead: A stochastic policy gradient averages over the action space, which in $d$ continuous dimensions needs a great many samples to estimate. The deterministic policy gradient does not integrate over actions at all — it follows the critic's gradient with respect to the action, which the critic can supply directly.

blocks.h: The gradient of the critic, not of a sample
blocks.b:
For a deterministic policy $a = \mu_\theta(s)$ the objective's gradient takes a chain-rule form:

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho}\Big[\nabla_\theta \mu_\theta(s) \; \nabla_a Q^{\mu}(s, a)\big|_{a = \mu_\theta(s)}\Big]$$

The critic is differentiated with respect to its action input, and that gradient is pushed back through the actor. Nothing is sampled over actions, so the estimator's variance does not grow with action dimensionality — which the paper demonstrates as an increasingly large advantage as $d$ rises.

The result was not obvious. It had been assumed the deterministic gradient did not exist in a usable form, since the expectation over actions is what the stochastic derivation relies on; the paper shows it is the limit of the stochastic gradient as the policy's variance goes to zero.

blocks.h: Why this is the answer for continuous actions
blocks.b:
Q-learning cannot be applied directly to a continuous action space, because acting requires $\arg\max_a Q(s,a)$ — itself a nonlinear optimisation, at every timestep. Discretising the actions makes the count exponential in the dimension.

The deterministic actor replaces that maximisation with a learned function. It is trained to output the action the critic scores highest, so at run time the $\arg\max$ is a forward pass. That reframing is what makes the whole continuous-control branch of this lane possible.

A deterministic policy explores nothing: given a state it always emits the same action, so without intervention the agent would never see alternatives.

DPG is therefore off-policy by construction. A separate stochastic behaviour policy — typically $\mu_\theta(s)$ plus noise — collects the data, and the deterministic target policy is learned from it. Because the actor's update does not involve an importance ratio over actions (there is no action distribution to reweight), the off-policy correction is far simpler than in the stochastic case.

That also means exploration is entirely a design choice outside the algorithm, and a bad one leaves the critic uninformed about the actions the actor is about to move towards.

blocks.h: What it needed to become practical
blocks.b:
The 2014 paper works with linear function approximation and modest problems. Applying it to neural networks runs straight into the instability that had blocked neural Q-learning for two decades, since a critic trained off-policy with a bootstrapped target and a function approximator is the deadly triad.

DDPG is the combination with DQN's stabilisers — a replay buffer and target networks — which is what made deterministic policy gradients work on high-dimensional continuous control from raw state and pixels. The overestimation that comes with an off-policy bootstrapped critic came too, and TD3 is the paper that addresses it.

refs.t: Deterministic Policy Gradient Algorithms
Policy Gradient Methods for Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation

ddpg.lead: DPG supplied a gradient for continuous actions and could not be trained with a neural critic without diverging. DDPG is the assembly: the deterministic policy gradient for the actor, DQN's replay buffer and target networks for the critic, and a softer form of the target update that suits the actor-critic coupling.

blocks.b:
The critic is trained by ordinary Q-learning regression, with the target computed from the target networks:

$$y = r + \gamma \, Q^-\big(s', \mu^-(s')\big)$$

The $\max$ over actions is replaced by the target actor's output, which is the whole point of the deterministic formulation. Replay decorrelates the samples and makes the method sample-efficient; target networks hold the regression target still.

The change from DQN is how the targets are updated. Instead of copying the weights every few thousand steps, DDPG uses a **soft** update, $\theta^- \leftarrow \tau\theta + (1-\tau)\theta^-$ with $\tau \approx 0.001$. Both actor and critic have targets and both are coupled, so a discrete jump in either perturbs the other; a slowly trailing average keeps the pair moving together. This became standard for actor-critic methods.

The actor is deterministic, so noise is added to its output during data collection. The paper uses an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process — temporally correlated noise, on the argument that physical control problems have momentum and independent per-step perturbations largely cancel.

Later work found uncorrelated Gaussian noise works about as well in most environments, which is a small illustration of how much of this lane's practice is empirical. Either way the exploration is a wrapper, tuned separately, with a scale that usually needs annealing — and it is the component SAC replaces by making stochasticity part of the objective.

DDPG solved a broad set of continuous-control tasks — locomotion, manipulation, driving — with the same architecture and hyperparameters, and did so from raw pixels as well as from state vectors. Before it, continuous control meant task-specific methods or heavily engineered policy classes.

Being off-policy is the practical advantage over the on-policy family: the replay buffer means each environment interaction is reused many times, which matters when interactions are expensive.

DDPG's reputation is for being difficult to get working, and the diagnosis came later. The critic is trained off-policy with a bootstrapped target and a function approximator, so Q-learning's overestimation bias applies — and here it is worse, because the actor is trained to **maximise** the critic, so it actively seeks out the actions the critic has overrated. Errors are not merely inherited but sought.

The result is a feedback loop: an overestimated action attracts the actor, the actor visits it, the critic's error is reinforced. Performance can collapse after appearing to converge, and results vary widely across random seeds — a reproducibility problem documented across the field around this time.

TD3 addresses exactly this with twin critics taking a minimum, delayed actor updates and target smoothing; SAC addresses it from the entropy side.

refs.t: Continuous control with deep reinforcement learning
Deterministic Policy Gradient Algorithms

td3.lead: DDPG's actor is trained to maximise its critic, so any action the critic overrates is an action the actor is pulled towards — overestimation is not merely inherited but actively sought. TD3 attacks it with three changes, each targeting one part of the loop that sustains it.

blocks.b:
Double DQN decouples selection from evaluation using a delayed copy of the network, and in an actor-critic setting that is too weak — the target and current networks are too similar for their errors to differ.

TD3 trains **two independent critics** from different initialisations and takes the minimum for the target:

$$y = r + \gamma \min_{i=1,2} Q^-_{\theta_i}\big(s', \tilde{a}\big)$$

The minimum is deliberately pessimistic. Where the two critics disagree — which is where at least one is wrong — it takes the lower estimate, so overestimation is suppressed at the price of a bias in the other direction. The paper argues that underestimation is the safer error, since it does not propagate: the actor is not drawn towards actions it undervalues, so nothing amplifies it.

**Delayed policy updates.** The actor is updated once every two critic updates, and the target networks likewise. A critic that is still badly wrong produces a badly wrong actor, whose data then makes the critic worse; letting the critic settle first breaks the coupling's tightest loop.

**Target policy smoothing.** Noise is added to the action used in the target:

$$\tilde{a} = \mu^-(s') + \mathrm{clip}(\varepsilon, -c, c), \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma)$$

This is a regulariser expressing that similar actions should have similar values. Without it, a narrow spike of overestimation in the critic — a sharp error at one action — is exactly what the actor will find and exploit. Averaging over a small neighbourhood makes such spikes unattractive.

The paper's method is worth noting. It measures the overestimation directly, plotting the critic's predicted value against the actual return achieved, and shows DDPG's estimate diverging far above what the policy obtains while TD3's tracks it.

That is the same diagnostic Double DQN used, applied to continuous control, and it is why the three changes are credible as a set: each is introduced with an ablation showing what it contributes, rather than as a bundle.

TD3 is markedly more stable than DDPG and became a standard baseline, but it is a collection of targeted fixes rather than a reformulation. Each brings a constant — the update delay, the smoothing noise scale and its clip — and the minimum over two critics is a blunt instrument whose pessimism is not tuned to how uncertain the critics actually are.

SAC arrives the same year from a different premise, deriving stochasticity from a maximum-entropy objective rather than adding it as smoothing, and also uses twin critics — which suggests the twin-critic minimum was the durable part of TD3 and the rest was scaffolding around DDPG's particular failure.

refs.t: Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods
Continuous control with deep reinforcement learning

sac.lead: DDPG and TD3 treat exploration as noise added to a deterministic policy, tuned by hand and annealed by a schedule. SAC changes the objective instead: reward the policy for staying uncertain, so stochasticity is something the agent optimises rather than something applied to it.

blocks.b:
The return is augmented with the policy's entropy at every step:

$$J(\pi) = \sum_t \mathbb{E}_{(s_t, a_t) \sim \rho_\pi}\Big[r(s_t, a_t) + \alpha \, \mathcal{H}\big(\pi(\cdot \mid s_t)\big)\Big]$$

The temperature $\alpha$ sets how much randomness is worth. The optimal policy is no longer a point but a distribution — energy-based, proportional to $\exp(Q(s,a)/\alpha)$ — so it assigns probability to every near-optimal action rather than committing to one.

Three consequences follow, and they are the paper's argument. Exploration is directed towards actions the critic thinks are plausible rather than uniformly random. Multiple ways of solving a task are all represented, so the policy is robust when one stops working. And the objective is smoother in the policy parameters, which makes optimisation better behaved than maximising a hard maximum.

SAC is off-policy with a replay buffer, twin critics with the minimum taken — TD3's mechanism, arrived at independently — and a stochastic actor.

The actor outputs a Gaussian which is squashed through $\tanh$ to respect action bounds, and is trained by the **reparameterisation** trick rather than by a score-function estimator: $a = \tanh(\mu_\theta(s) + \sigma_\theta(s) \odot \epsilon)$, so the critic's gradient flows through the sampled action into the policy parameters directly. That is the same mechanism DPG uses, extended to a stochastic policy, and it is much lower variance than REINFORCE-style estimation.

The policy loss is a KL divergence to the exponentiated Q-function, which reduces in practice to maximising $\mathbb{E}[Q(s,a) - \alpha \log \pi(a|s)]$ — the critic's opinion, penalised by how confident the policy is.

$\alpha$ is the one delicate hyperparameter: too high and the policy is aimlessly random, too low and it collapses to a deterministic one. Worse, the right value changes during training and across tasks, since it trades against the reward scale.

The follow-up paper removes it by making the entropy a **constraint** rather than a term — require $\mathbb{E}[-\log \pi(a|s)] \geq \bar{\mathcal{H}}$ for a target entropy, and update $\alpha$ by dual gradient descent on the resulting Lagrangian. The target is set from the action dimensionality, so nothing task-specific remains.

That change is most of why SAC became the default continuous-control algorithm: it is off-policy, sample-efficient, and works across tasks without per-task tuning, which none of its predecessors managed.

SAC is strong in simulation and still needs on the order of a million environment steps for a locomotion task, which for physical robots is a great deal. It is also off-policy with a bootstrapped critic and a function approximator — the deadly triad — so its stability rests on the twin-critic minimum and the entropy term rather than on any guarantee.

The entropy bonus itself distorts the objective: the policy being optimised is not the one that maximises reward, and at deployment one usually takes the mean action rather than sampling, which is a policy the training never optimised.

And because the critic is trained only on data in the buffer, actions far from what has been tried are unconstrained — the failure that becomes decisive when the buffer is fixed rather than growing, which is what CQL exists to address.

alphago.lead: Go had resisted the tree search that solved chess: the branching factor is an order of magnitude larger and no hand-written function could evaluate a position. AlphaGo supplies both missing pieces with neural networks — a policy to narrow the search and a value network to evaluate positions — and puts them inside Monte Carlo tree search.

blocks.b:
Exhaustive search is $b^d$ in branching factor and depth, and Go's $b \approx 250$ over $d \approx 150$ puts it far beyond reach. Two reductions are needed and both had been unavailable.

**Breadth** is reduced by a policy network that proposes plausible moves, so the search expands a small fraction of the legal ones. **Depth** is reduced by a value network that estimates the outcome from a position, so a line can be truncated rather than played to the end.

Chess programs had a hand-written evaluation function for the second. For Go, decades of effort produced nothing adequate — the value of a position depends on global structure that resists local features — which is why the game was the standing benchmark for the field.

A **supervised policy network** is trained on human expert games to predict the next move, reaching around $57\%$ accuracy. A fast rollout policy, a small linear model, is trained the same way for use inside simulations where speed matters more than strength.

The supervised network is then improved by **self-play** with policy gradients, producing an RL policy network that beats its supervised parent overwhelmingly.

A **value network** is trained by regression to predict the outcome of positions from self-play games of the RL policy. The paper notes that training it on complete games overfits — successive positions in one game are highly correlated and share a label — so the dataset is built from one position per self-play game, thirty million games.

MCTS selects moves by a variant of PUCT, balancing the value accumulated so far against the policy's prior and the visit count:

$$a_t = \arg\max_a \Big( Q(s,a) + c \, P(s,a) \frac{\sqrt{\sum_b N(s,b)}}{1 + N(s,a)} \Big)$$

The prior $P$ concentrates the search on moves the policy likes; the visit-count term ensures under-explored moves are eventually tried. Leaf positions are evaluated by a **mixture** of the value network and the outcome of a fast rollout to the end, which the paper finds better than either alone.

The combination is what wins. Search corrects the policy's mistakes, and the policy makes search affordable — neither alone was close to professional strength.

AlphaGo beat Fan Hui and then Lee Sedol, which was the field's most visible result of the decade. Its pipeline is nonetheless elaborate and dependent in ways the successors removed.

It begins from human games, so its priors inherit human preferences and its ceiling is influenced by them. It uses several networks with different roles, trained in stages, plus a hand-engineered fast rollout policy and hand-crafted input features beyond the raw board. And it needs a perfect simulator of the rules to search with.

AlphaGo Zero removes the human data, the rollouts and the separate networks; AlphaZero removes the game-specific components; MuZero removes the requirement for the rules themselves.
