vid2world.lead: A world model has always been trained on the thing it models: video of an environment together with the actions that produced it, collected on purpose and never cheaply. Video diffusion models are trained on the internet, know far more about how the world moves, and are useless as world models for two structural reasons — they see the whole clip at once, and nothing tells them what the agent did. Vid2World is the surgery that removes both, performed on a 1.4B pre-trained model and checked on robot manipulation, a 3D shooter and open-world navigation.

blocks.h: Causalising a convolution without discarding what it knew
blocks.b:
Temporal attention is the easy half. Apply a causal mask and stop. A dot product does not care how long the sequence is, so restricting the receptive field to the past changes nothing about how the surviving query-key relations are computed, and no parameter moves.

Temporal convolution is the hard half, because a symmetric kernel $\{w_t\}_{t=-m}^{m}$ reads the future by construction. Three transfers are compared:

**Shift** moves the whole kernel $m$ steps into the past. Every weight survives and every one is misaligned — position $i$ now aggregates timestep $i-m$, with no guarantee the representation resembles the old one.

**Masked** keeps $\{w_t\}_{t=-m}^{0}$ and zeroes the rest, a hard causal mask applied at initialisation. Causal, and it throws away whatever the future-facing weights had learned.

**Extrapolative**, the paper's, starts from the observation that a future feature is locally close to a linear function of the past $p$ features, $z_{t+k} \approx \sum_{j} \gamma_{k,j} z_{t-j} + \beta_k$, and redistributes the future weights onto the past ones accordingly:

$$w'_j = \mathbb{1}_{[j\ge -m]}\,w_j + \mathbb{1}_{[-p+1\le j\le 0]}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\gamma_{i,-j}\,w_i$$

$$b' = b + \sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i\,\beta_i$$

The criterion it is derived from is worth stating, because it is the whole difference from the other two: preserve the layer's **output**, $\sum_i w_i z_{t+i} + b = \sum_j w'_j z_{t+j} + b'$, rather than preserve its weights.

blocks.h: Independent noise per frame is what makes the rollout possible
blocks.b:
Architecture alone does not get there. At inference the noise levels along the sequence are $(0, 0, \dots, 0, k)$: a fully denoised history and one frame in progress. A model trained the conventional way — one noise level shared by every frame — has never once seen that combination, and it is the only combination that ever occurs during a rollout.

So training samples $k_t \sim \mathcal{U}(0,K)$ independently for every frame, which is Diffusion Forcing. That exposes the model to the entire space of level combinations rather than the diagonal of it, and the causal rollout becomes something the model has practised instead of something it is asked to improvise.

blocks.h: Action guidance, and what it is guidance towards
blocks.b:
Conditioning first: the embedding of $a_{t-1}$ passes through a small MLP and is added to the latent at temporal position $t$, so each frame is conditioned on the action that preceded it and on no later one. Video-level action embeddings — the whole sequence squeezed into one vector, in the manner of a text prompt — cannot do this, and cannot accept actions arriving one at a time either.

Then guidance. Each action is dropped independently with probability $p$ during training, which teaches the model the score both with and without the most recent action, and inference composes them:

$$\epsilon_{\text{guided}} = (1+\lambda)\,\epsilon_{\text{cond}} - \lambda\,\epsilon_{\text{ucond}}$$

The paper's theorem says what that composition actually samples from. Writing $H_t$ for the history excluding the current action,

$$\tilde p(x_t \mid a_{t-1}, H_t) \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(x_t \mid H_t)}_{\text{history-consistent prior}} \cdot \underbrace{p(a_{t-1}\mid x_t, H_t)^{\omega}}_{\text{action alignment}}$$

— a prior that respects the past times an implicit classifier that asks whether the frame looks like the consequence of the action. $\lambda$ is then a dial for responsiveness at test time, which is the property a world model is judged on: not average behaviour, but what happens *because of this action*.

blocks.h: What it buys, and the twenty seconds
blocks.b:
The backbone is DynamiCrafter, 1.4B parameters, itself fine-tuned from VideoCrafter — an image-to-video latent diffusion model, not a world model of any kind. Transferred, it beats both the existing transfer recipes and the state-of-the-art domain-specific world models on RT-1 robot manipulation, Counter-Strike game simulation and RECON open-world navigation. Training is four A100s, 100k steps, seven days, 37GB.

The cost is recorded rather than buried. One A100, ten history frames, 50-step DDIM, batch of two: **20.0 seconds per generated frame**. The paper lists the ways out — fewer steps, shorter history, JIT compilation, a rolling KV cache — and its own discussion section points at one-step generative models as the structural fix, citing MeanFlow among them.

Two failure modes are shown rather than described, and both are the same shape. The arm moves in the right direction and the gripper's control of the green bag is not predicted; the movement is right and the grasped object is quietly swapped for a more familiar one. A model that has watched the internet knows what usually happens, which is exactly the prior that has to be overruled when the question is what happens *this* time.

astra.lead: Astra and Vid2World start from the same observation and arrive somewhere different. Both take a pre-trained video diffusion model and make it answer to actions. What Astra contributes is what it found on the way: conditioning on more history makes the video more coherent and makes the model stop listening. It names that **visual inertia**, and the fix is to blur the memory on purpose.

blocks.h: Chunk-wise autoregressive denoising on a backbone that mostly does not move
blocks.b:
The factorisation is the ordinary one, over chunks rather than frames:

$$p(z^{1:N}) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} p\big(z^{i} \mid z^{<i}\big)$$

and each chunk is produced by flow matching, with the history concatenated along the temporal dimension before the transformer reads it:

$$z^i_t = (1-t)z^i_0 + t\,\epsilon, \qquad \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\big\|v_\theta(z^i_t, t \mid z^{<i}) - v^{*}\big\|_2^2$$

The backbone is Wan 2.1 at 1.3B and almost all of it is frozen — only the self-attention layers train. Actions enter through the **ACT-Adapter**: an encoder projects them into the video latent space and the result is added element-wise at every block, with a single linear layer initialised to the identity inserted after each self-attention block, so the first optimisation step changes nothing and the pre-trained function is the starting point rather than a casualty. **366.8M trainable parameters**, against Yume's full tuning of Wan2.1-14B and Matrix-Game's 1.8B.

Then guidance, in CFG's shape with the action as the dropped condition:

$$v_{\text{guided}} = v_\theta(z_t,t,\varnothing) + s\big(v_\theta(z_t,t,a) - v_\theta(z_t,t,\varnothing)\big)$$

blocks.h: Visual inertia, and noise used as a mask
blocks.b:
The trade-off is measured, not assumed. Train Astra at increasing history lengths with the fix removed and the action-following score falls as context grows. The cause is in the data rather than the architecture: real video is overwhelmingly smooth motion, so continuity is almost always the better bet, and a dense clean visual context out-votes a sparse action signal. A model that has learned this is not broken — it is correct on average and useless to steer.

Yume masks visual tokens. Astra injects random noise into the conditioning frames instead — **noise as mask** — which needs no architectural change and no new parameters, and which stops the model copying clean frames forward because there are no clean frames to copy. The corruption noise is independent of the diffusion noise, so inference still runs on a clean history. The horizon is then extended by FramePack's compression: keep the first frame, squeeze the middle into compact tokens.

The ablation is the strongest number in the paper and it has a wrinkle worth stating. Removing the noise takes instruction following from **0.669 to 0.359** — by far the largest single drop, larger than removing action-free guidance (0.545), the adapter (0.642) or the expert routing (0.651). The wrinkle is that the consistency metrics do not improve when it is removed either: subject consistency falls 0.939 → 0.903, background 0.945 → 0.927. The trade-off it was introduced to break shows up against *history length*, not against this switch.

blocks.h: A mixture of experts, where the tokens are actions
blocks.b:
Camera pose, robot pose and keyboard-and-mouse commands differ in dimension, in scale and in what they mean. Each modality gets its own projector into a shared space, $\tilde a^i = R_m(a^i_m)$; a router scores the result and selects the top $K$ experts, each an MLP; the outputs are combined by gate weight.

$$g^i = \mathrm{Router}(\tilde a^i), \qquad e^i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} g^i_k\, E_k(\tilde a^i)$$

A binary flag is appended marking whether the entry is a past action or the current one. This is what lets a single checkpoint train across roughly **397K clips — 360 hours** — of nuScenes, Sekai, SpatialVID, RT-1 and Multi-Cam Video, whose action formats have nothing in common. The ablation without it had to be trained on camera-action data alone, *since it cannot process other modalities*, which is the point made as an experimental constraint.

The paper is candid about the price: joint training on heterogeneous data slightly reduces performance on any single scenario, and buys cross-domain generalisation with it.

Astra-Bench holds out 20 samples from each dataset; everything is generated at 480×832, 20 FPS, 96 frames, 50 steps. Instruction following **0.669**, against Yume's 0.652, Matrix-Game's 0.268 and Wan-2.1's 0.061 — the last of which is the honest measure of how much a text-to-video model responds to an action, which is barely at all. Subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness and aesthetic quality all lead as well. Imaging quality is the one column it does not win: 0.747 against Matrix-Game's 0.748. Instruction following is scored by human raters rather than by pose estimation, because MegaSaM's camera-motion predictions are not accurate enough to grade with.

Trained on 8 GPUs of 80GB for 30 epochs, about 24 hours. The interaction horizon is 8–10 seconds, matching Yume and well past Wan-2.1's few seconds.

The limitation is stated in the paper's own words and it is the same one Vid2World has: diffusion plus autoregressive rollout means several denoising steps per frame, real-time deployment is out of reach, and with it the latency-sensitive uses — online control, interactive robotics — that a world model exists to serve. The route it proposes is distillation, which is the road Self Forcing and MotionStream had already taken for video without actions.

adaworld.lead: Every world model in this track was trained on video paired with the actions that produced it, and the pairing is the expensive half — it has to be logged by an instrumented environment, and each environment logs a different vocabulary. AdaWorld's claim is that the pairing can be manufactured. An autoencoder squeezed through a narrow enough bottleneck recovers, from two consecutive frames and nothing else, a vector that behaves like the action taken between them. Pretrain on two billion frames conditioned on those vectors and adapting to a real control scheme stops being training and becomes initialisation.

blocks.h: The bottleneck is not a component of the method, it is the method
blocks.b:
The latent action autoencoder takes two consecutive frames $f_{t:t+1}$ and returns one vector. The encoder is the spatiotemporal Transformer Genie introduced — interleaved spatial and temporal attention, rotary embeddings on the temporal axis — with two learnable tokens $a_{t:t+1}$ appended. After the attention blocks every token is discarded except $a_{t+1}$, which is projected to a Gaussian posterior $(\mu_{\tilde a}, \sigma_{\tilde a})$. A sample $\tilde a$ is attached to $f_t$ and a *spatial* Transformer must predict $f_{t+1}$ in pixel space from that alone:

$$\mathcal{L}^{\text{pred}}_{\theta,\phi}(f_{t+1}) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\tilde a \mid f_{t:t+1})} \log p_\theta(f_{t+1} \mid \tilde a, f_t) - \beta\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(\tilde a \mid f_{t:t+1}) \,\|\, p(\tilde a)\right)$$

The argument for why $\tilde a$ ends up meaning something is a counting argument. The latent is extremely small next to a frame, so it cannot smuggle the frame through; the only way to reduce the prediction error is to spend it on whatever changed. Where the dominant change in a scene is what the agent did — which is the standing assumption of this whole line of work — that is the action, expressed independently of the context it happened in.

$\beta$ is what makes it adjustable, and it is a genuine trade-off rather than a knob left at a default. At the standard VAE's $\beta = 1$ the posterior is constrained too hard and the latents cannot express diverse transitions; drop it too far and disentanglement goes with it. A UMAP of latents collected from Habitat, Minecraft and DMLab settles it: at $\beta = 2\times 10^{-4}$ the same action taken in three unrelated environments lands in the same cluster, and at a lower $\beta$ the latents separate more cleanly *within* an environment while the overlap *across* environments disappears — which is exactly the property being bought.

blocks.h: Continuous, and what the discrete version actually costs
blocks.b:
Genie's latent action model quantises: a VQ codebook of eight discrete codes. AdaWorld implements precisely that as one of its three baselines, holding everything else fixed, so the comparison is about the parameterisation and nothing else.

The evaluation is action transfer — extract a latent action sequence from a demonstration video, apply it to the first frame of a *different* video of the same labelled action, and ask whether the demonstrated action happened. On 1300 pairs drawn from LIBERO and Something-Something v2, with four volunteers judging 50 pairs from each, the human verdicts are the column worth reading. Action-agnostic pretraining transfers the action **0%** of the time on LIBERO and 1% on SSv2. Conditioning on optical flow reaches 2% and 10.5%. The discrete eight-code variant reaches **3.5%** and 21.5%. AdaWorld reaches **70.5%** and 61.5%.

FVD tells the same story more quietly — 767.0 against the discrete variant's 1504.5 on LIBERO, 473.4 against 726.8 on SSv2 — but the human numbers are the ones that separate *nearly working* from *not working*. Eight codes carry enough to beat doing nothing and not enough to carry an action across a context change, which on LIBERO is only a rearrangement of the objects on the table.

Continuity then buys two things a codebook cannot. Latent actions for the same label can be **averaged**, and the average is a usable prototype — which is what every adaptation in the paper initialises from. And two actions can be **interpolated**: the midpoint of the latents for right and jump produces jumping to the right, an action the model was never told about.

blocks.h: One frame at a time, on a backbone borrowed from video generation
blocks.b:
Reusing the autoencoder's decoder as the world model is the obvious move and it fails — one forward pass makes a coarse prediction, and the error compounds visibly after a few interactions. So the world model is separate and it is a diffusion model, initialised from Stable Video Diffusion.

The modification to SVD is the point. SVD denoises a clip; AdaWorld denoises **one frame**, which is what makes the control frame-level instead of clip-level and lets an action arrive per step. The latent action is concatenated onto both the timestep embedding and the CLIP image embedding, the last frame in memory becomes SVD's conditioning image, and up to six historical frames are encoded with SVD's own image encoder and concatenated to the noise latent. The number of history frames is sampled randomly during training and passed in as a condition, so a short memory at inference is a case the model has seen.

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{pretrain}} = \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\epsilon,t}\left[\left\| x_0 - \hat x_0(x_t, t, c) \right\|^2\right]$$

History frames are corrupted with noise augmentation during training and left clean at inference, which is the standard defence against long-term drift — and, incidentally, the same instinct Astra would later push much harder for a different reason.

The pretraining mixture is about 2000M frames, and its shape is more interesting than its size. Gym Retro supplies 1000M frames at 49%, a thousand ROMs pulled off the web and driven by an automated agent, so the largest and cheapest source is old console games. Open X-Embodiment is 170M frames at 30%, real robot footage weighted about three and a half times above its share of the frames. Ego4D contributes 330M frames and is sampled at **1%**. A data-diversity ablation explains the weighting: adding OpenX to a Gym Retro mixture improves the latent action decoder on Procgen, a 2D game benchmark that resembles neither — real robot video generalises to virtual games.

blocks.h: Eight hundred steps, and the three things it still cannot do
blocks.b:
Adaptation is deliberately starved: 100 samples per discrete action, 800 finetuning steps, batch 32, learning rate $5\times 10^{-5}$ with the pretrained weights discounted by a factor of ten. The $N$ action embeddings of the new environment are initialised with the averaged latent actions inferred from those samples. On four environments absent from pretraining — Habitat, Minecraft, DMLab and nuScenes — AdaWorld leads on PSNR and LPIPS everywhere.

But the honest reading of that table is not the ranking. Every action-aware variant beats the action-agnostic baseline by a wide margin — 20.34 to 23.58 PSNR on Habitat — and among the action-aware variants the discrete one is close behind at 23.31. The large effect is *conditioning on an inferred action at all*; the parameterisation is a second-order refinement, and it only becomes decisive under the context shift the transfer table measured.

Planning is where the gap reopens. Goal-reaching over 30 scenes in each of four Procgen games, sampling-based MPC optimised by the cross-entropy method, averaged over five seeds: random planning succeeds 26.17% of the time and the action-agnostic world model 26.00%, which is to say it contributes nothing. A Q-table built from the same samples manages 27.17%. AdaWorld reaches **44.83%** without updating a single weight — substituting averaged latent actions for the action embeddings and nothing else — and **56.67%** after 500 steps of finetuning, against an oracle that plans with the true simulator at 80.67%.

One inconsistency is left in view rather than smoothed: on Jumper, finetuning *hurts*, 68.00% down to 58.67%. On the VP² robot benchmark the aggregate success is 21.54 against the action-agnostic 5.03. And conditioning iVideoGPT — a different architecture entirely, autoregressive rather than diffusion — on the same latent actions during its pretraining improves it too, 16.59 to 17.40 PSNR on BAIR, which is the evidence that this is a pretraining paradigm rather than one model's trick.

The limitations are stated plainly. It does not run at real time. It cannot invent much once a rollout leaves the initial scene. Extremely long rollouts are beyond it. The failure figure adds real-world physics, dynamic agents and large view changes to the list.

olafworld.lead: AdaWorld's promise was a control interface read off unlabelled video, and it delivers one that works inside the material it was trained on. Olaf-World's contribution is the diagnosis of why it does not travel. The objective only ever compares a latent to the frame it produced, within one clip, so nothing in the whole of training ever asks whether turn left in a kitchen points the same direction in latent space as turn left in a street. Actions are unobserved; their effects are not. And an effect measured in a frozen encoder's feature space is comparable across every video there is, which is enough to give the latents a shared coordinate system.

blocks.h: Two failure modes, and only the first one is obvious
blocks.b:
A latent action model pairs a causal inverse-dynamics encoder $q_\phi(z_i \mid x_{0:i+1})$ with a forward decoder $p_\theta(x_{i+1} \mid x_i, z_i)$, trained step-wise:

$$\mathcal{L}^{\text{VAE}}_{\theta,\phi} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}\Big[-\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z_i \mid x_{0:i+1})}\log p_\theta(x_{i+1}\mid x_i, z_i) + \beta\,\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z_i \mid x_{0:i+1})\,\|\,p(z_i)\big)\Big]$$

**Shortcut learning** is the failure everyone already knows. The posterior is conditioned on $x_{i+1}$, so a sufficiently expressive decoder can cut the loss by encoding context-dependent cues that happen to correlate with the next frame rather than a transferable control. A tighter bottleneck, motion-weighted objectives and latent-space constraints all attack this, and AdaWorld's $\beta$ is one of them.

**Cross-context non-identifiability** is the failure none of them touch, because all of those remedies operate within a clip. The loss never compares latents across trajectories. Nothing fixes the orientation of the latent coordinate system, so it is free to drift from video to video: the same semantic motion may map to different directions of the space in different scenes, and every one of those assignments has exactly the same training loss. The model is not making a mistake — the objective simply never asked the question.

That is why a constraint has to be **sequence-level and external**. It needs a reference that exists outside any single clip and means the same thing in all of them.

blocks.h: The alignment term, and the direction it points in
blocks.b:
Let $f$ be a frozen self-supervised video encoder — V-JEPA 2's ViT by default — producing spatiotemporal tokens that are spatially pooled to a per-frame descriptor $s_i \in \mathbb{R}^D$. The clip's **effect direction** is the net feature change over its window:

$$\tau_* = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}\left(s_{i+1} - s_i\right) \in \mathbb{R}^D$$

Because it is built from temporal differences and then averaged, static appearance largely cancels and coherent motion survives. On the control side the inferred latents are integrated the same way and lifted into the encoder's space by a trainable head:

$$\bar z = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=0}^{K-1} z_i, \qquad u = h_\psi(\bar z) \in \mathbb{R}^D$$

$$\mathcal{L}^{\text{Seq}\Delta\text{-REPA}}_{\psi} = 1 - \left\langle \mathrm{norm}(u),\, \mathrm{norm}(\tau_*) \right\rangle$$

and the whole thing is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{LAM}} = \mathcal{L}^{\text{VAE}}_{\theta,\phi} + \lambda\,\mathcal{L}^{\text{Seq}\Delta\text{-REPA}}_{\psi}$ with $\lambda = 0.02$, window $K = 16$ and $d_z = 32$, the encoder $f$ frozen throughout.

The name is borrowed from REPA and the direction is not. REPA and its video successors align a generator's *internal features* to a pretrained encoder's features — feature to feature — to make the generator's representations better and its training faster. Here the generator's internals are never touched. What is aligned is a **control** to an **effect**: the thing you would press against the change pressing it produces. That is why the target is a difference and not a state, and why the loss is a cosine rather than a distance — the claim is about direction, not magnitude, and feature norms vary across domains in ways that would otherwise leak straight back in.

The world model on top is conventional by design, so the comparison isolates the objective: a pretrained SkyReels-V2-1.3B image-to-video DiT, flow matching, latent actions projected and added to the diffusion timestep embedding, then fed to per-block AdaLN-Zero modulation. Because the 3D video VAE compresses time by $r=4$, four consecutive per-step actions are grouped into one conditioning vector.

blocks.h: Does the space mean the same thing twice
blocks.b:
The test environment is chosen so the question can actually be asked. MIND supplies two disjoint subsets recorded in Unreal Engine 5 — first-person and third-person — with different scenes and different camera rigs but the **same eight-action label space**: W/S/A/D for movement and four look directions. So a probe trained on one and evaluated on the other measures exactly the quantity in dispute, and AdaWorld is re-run on the same backbone, data and adaptation budget with only its latent-action training left as its own.

Train a linear probe to predict the eight actions from $z_t$, select the checkpoint on in-domain validation, then apply that same probe to the other subset. In macro-F1, AdaWorld scores 0.6004 in-domain on first-person and **0.4820** transferred to third-person; Olaf-World scores 0.8138 and **0.6250**. Going the other way the gap is wider still where it matters most: on third-person in-domain AdaWorld saturates at 0.4827 while Olaf-World reaches **0.8256**.

The prototype figure says the same thing more directly. Compute a class centroid per action within each domain and take the cross-domain cosine similarity matrix. AdaWorld's is high nearly everywhere — each first-person action looks like several third-person actions at once, which is precisely what non-identifiability predicts. Olaf-World's is diagonal-dominant, matching actions retaining similarity while non-matching pairs fall to zero or below.

The residual confusion is instructive and the paper does not hide it: the yaw looks, ← and →, stay muddled. That is not a defect of the alignment but a fact about the rigs — the same key produces genuinely different observable motion from an egocentric camera than from one following a character, and a method that anchors to observable effect will inherit that ambiguity by construction.

Downstream, controllability follows. Measured by relative pose error against the commanded actions, Olaf-World has the lowest translational and rotational error in all six settings — zero, one and fifty adaptation videos, on both subsets. At fifty videos on third-person that is 0.0222 and 0.2082 against AdaWorld's 0.0393 and 0.3353.

blocks.h: What the reference has to be, and what did not get better
blocks.b:
Swap the frozen encoder and the method's dependence becomes visible. Under a shortened ten-epoch schedule, V-JEPA 2 reaches 0.7044 in-domain macro-F1 and VideoMAE V2 0.6626, while **DINOv3 — an image encoder — manages 0.2334 against the no-alignment baseline's 0.1849**. Aligning to a representation with no temporal structure is very nearly the same as not aligning at all, which is the sharpest available confirmation that the signal lives in the *difference* between frames rather than in the features themselves. That two video encoders with unrelated pretraining objectives both work says the method is not tied to a particular backbone.

The same table contains a wrinkle worth reporting because the paper reports it: on that short schedule V-JEPA 2's cross-domain 1st→3rd score is 0.2972, *below* VideoMAE V2's 0.4697, so the default encoder is not uniformly the best one. The ablation of the objective has a matching honesty — dropping the $\ell_2$ normalisation scores 0.5934 on 3rd→1st against the full objective's 0.5904, one column of four where removing a component wins, narrowly, and it is printed rather than dropped.

And then the thing that did not improve. At zero adaptation videos Olaf-World is slightly *behind* AdaWorld on image quality, 0.5400 against 0.5600, and on temporal consistency, 0.9123 against 0.9226. Under unseen visual contexts its rotational error of 1.2221 barely beats conditioning directly on ground-truth actions at 1.2343, though AdaWorld degrades badly there at 1.7063. The paper's own phrasing is comparable video quality, and the accurate summary is narrower than the headline: Seq$\Delta$-REPA buys **control**, not pixels. That is what it was designed to buy, and a reader who came for a better picture should be told so.

The failure cases have a common shape — the model resolves a conflict in favour of executing the command. A transferred action that would drive into an obstacle produces a scene quietly rearranged so the obstacle is gone. An action implying an event, such as a character entering, has no way to specify *which* character, and comes out as background drift instead: a plausible relative-motion reading of the control, and not the event that was meant.
